West Pokot takes KICOSCA mantle as 13th edition games kick off
items.description: West Pokot takes KICOSCA mantle as 13th edition games kick off Kenya News Agency West Pokot reinforces security ahead of KICOSCA games Kenya News Agency West Pokot’s Kachapin takes over KICOSCA patronage as Orengo’s tenure ends TV47 Digital Makueni Joins Counties for KICOSCA 13th Edition as Team Targets Strong Performance Makueni County Government Why Kajiado County has withdrawn 7 teams from KICOSCA Games Mozzart Sport Kenya
content: West Pokot Governor Simon Kachapin has officially assumed the patronage of the Kenya Inter-Counties Sports and Cultural Association (KICOSCA), pledging to strengthen the association and promote sports, cultural exchange and employee welfare across the 47 counties.

Kachapin received the Chain of Authority and Torch from outgoing patron, Siaya Governor James Orengo, during a handover ceremony at the official Governor’s Residence in Kapenguria before proceeding to Makutano Stadium for the official opening of the 13th edition of the games on Monday.

The week-long competition, running from November 23 to 28, has brought together county government employees, athletes, cultural performers and officials from across the country under the theme, “Promoting National Cohesion and Peaceful Co-existence through Sports and Culture.”

The event has attracted thousands of spectators, with 39 counties having confirmed participation, making it an important national platform for bringing Kenyans together through sports and cultural exchange.
The colourful opening ceremony was attended by County Commissioner Benson Leparmorijo, Deputy Governors Robert Komolle(West Pokot), Philomena Kapkory (Trans Nzoia) and Wilberforce Kitiezo (Vihiga).
Others present included Members of Parliament Samuel Moroto and Titus Lotee, County Secretaries from Mombasa and Nyandarua, Members of County Assemblies and other county government officials.

In his acceptance speech, Kachapin described the patronage as a responsibility to provide leadership and strengthen the association, saying the instruments handed over to him carried significant institutional and symbolic meaning.
“Today, I am not simply receiving ceremonial items; I am accepting a responsibility and a mandate to serve the KICOSCA fraternity,” said Kachapin.
He explained that the Chain of Authority represented leadership, trust and responsibility, while the Torch symbolize hope, inspiration and the transfer of vision from one leadership to another.

The governor pledged to work closely with the Council of Governors, the KICOSCA National Executive Committee and all member counties to strengthen the association through wider participation in sporting and cultural activities.

He further called for stronger institutional partnerships and sustained programmes to promote the welfare and wellness of county employees, noting that KICOSCA should remain active throughout the year rather than being limited to annual competitions.
Outgoing patron Governor Orengo, who presided over the handover, pledged his support to Kachapin.
Reflecting on Siaya’s hosting of the 12th edition, Orengo described sports as a powerful instrument for national unity, wellness and grassroots economic transformation.
“Sports are not just games, they are a powerful catalyst for national unity, wellness, and grassroots economic transformation,” he said.
He urged county governments to invest in sporting infrastructure, talent academies and financial support for athletes to establish sustainable systems that nurture talent beyond annual competitions.
Orengo also challenged participants to uphold discipline, integrity and fair play, saying his commitment to championing sports development across the 47 counties remained solid.
Kachapin said hosting the games was a historic milestone for West Pokot stressing it marked the first time the county was hosting the national event since the advent of devolution in 2013.

He noted that the games offered an opportunity to showcase the county’s cultural heritage, hospitality and economic potential while strengthening relationships among Kenyans from different backgrounds.
“Sports are much more than competition, medals and trophies. They promote good health, discipline, teamwork, friendship and mutual respect,” he said.

The governor highlighted his administration’s investment in grassroots sports, including support for local football leagues and the Kaptabuk High Altitude Athletics Camp in Lelan, which provides athletes with opportunities to develop their abilities and compete at higher levels.

He also cited ongoing improvements to sporting facilities, including the development of Makutano Stadium, saying the county intended to establish modern facilities capable of hosting major sporting events.
Beyond competition, Kachapin said the games would stimulate local economic activities through increased demand for accommodation, transport, food and other services.
He urged traders, hotel operators, transport providers and food vendors to take advantage of the influx of visitors, noting that the event should leave behind lasting economic opportunities.
County Commissioner Benson Leparmorijo assured residents, visitors and business operators of enhanced security throughout the games period.
He said all security agencies had been mobilized and were working together under a multi-agency arrangement to protect participants and members of the public.
He urged residents to embrace visitors and support the event, noting that the games presented an opportunity for West Pokot to showcase its hospitality, culture and economic potential.
The opening programme got underway with a women’s tug-of-war contest between Kakamega and Bomet, followed by the men’s contest pitting hosts West Pokot against Kisumu.
A football encounter between West Pokot and Busia followed, with the hosts registering a convincing 3-1 victory to the excitement of their home supporters.
Having won the championship in the last three consecutive editions, West Pokot will be seeking to extend its winning streak and defend its title on home soil.
The games also provide an important platform for identifying and selecting national representatives for the forthcoming East Africa Local Authorities Sports and Cultural Association (EALASCA) Games.

Kachapin urged athletes and cultural performers to compete with passion while respecting their opponents, observing that friendships established and national unity strengthened would be more valuable than trophies.
He expressed optimism that the 13th edition would open a new chapter in sporting excellence, institutional wellness, cultural exchange and national cohesion.

items.title: Unregulated early campaigns put Kenya’s electoral process to the test
items.description: Despite a court ruling outlawing out-of-season electioneering, political impunity and government inaction threaten the 2027 vote and public safety.
content: Published on 24 November 2026 in ISS Today
By Guyo Chepe Turi Research Officer, East Africa Peace and Security Governance, ISS Nairobi

Kenya appears to be in a constant state of electioneering, with campaigns starting as soon as new leaders are sworn in and intensifying as the next election approaches. More than eight months before the 10 August 2027 general election, politicians are mobilising support nationwide, despite a court ruling declaring campaigning before 29 May 2027 unconstitutional.

This culture of constant campaigning has created anxiety among citizens and disrupted daily life. Clashes between supporters of opposing groups continue to cause significant economic losses by interrupting trade and supply chains.

Early campaigns have also led to destruction of property and increased political violence across the country. There have been attacks on businesses such as hotels suspected of hosting rival political camps. This violence has even affected worshippers at religious gatherings where political leaders in attendance were the main targets.

The Kenya Human Rights Commission recorded 284 incidents of human rights violence across the country between January and July 2026, with the Kenya Police Service identified as the main perpetrator. This has put the spotlight on how police restore public order during demonstrations.
Blame-trading, with little accountability for those behind political violence, has left citizens vulnerable

Citing repeated armed attacks since early 2025, human rights groups have sued senior security officials, accusing them of allowing violence targeting political, religious and civic gatherings to continue despite warnings. They also accuse the officials of failing to identify and prosecute the financiers, recruiters and perpetrators of organised political gangs, despite investigative reports documenting these syndicates.

Security agencies, for their part, have repeatedly blamed political leaders for financing violence ahead of the 2027 election. Members of the National Assembly dispute this, instead accusing the police of shielding politicians linked to funding criminal gangs .

Responding to questions in the National Assembly, Interior and National Administration Cabinet Secretary Kipchumba Murkomen in turn blamed the judiciary for releasing suspects on lenient bail terms and favouring politicians arrested over political violence.
Such trading of blame, with little accountability for those behind political violence, has left citizens vulnerable to attacks at political gatherings.

Early campaigns also allow politicians to make repeated statements likely to undermine the electoral process. On 11 September, shortly after launching his gubernatorial bid in Mombasa, United Democratic Alliance Secretary-General Hassan Omar suggested dead voters’ fingerprints could be used to cast votes in favour of President William Ruto.
The Election Offences Act and Electoral Code of Conduct are enforceable only during the campaign period

Omar was summoned to appear before the Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission’s Electoral Code of Conduct Enforcement Committee on 21 October over the remarks. The committee later found him in breach of the Electoral Code of Conduct and issued a formal warning.
Such statements, made outside the official campaign period, stir controversy and are likely to cast doubt on the credibility of next year’s election.

A June 2025 court ruling declared campaigning outside the official campaign period unconstitutional. It said early campaigns violate the rights to life, freedom from violence, development and free and fair elections. The ruling also directed the Attorney General to draft legislation within 12 months to govern political campaigns outside the official period. That deadline has passed, and the legislation has yet to be drafted.

The Election Offences Act, 2016 and the Electoral Code of Conduct are enforceable only during the official campaign period – in this case 29 May to 7 August 2027 – leaving a legal gap that the court’s directive was meant to close.

The absence of legislation and a deep sense of impunity have given the political class a blank cheque to campaign in defiance of the law. Kenyan politics is also lucrative: Members of Parliament earn over US$10 000 per month, along with other hefty benefits . These rewards fuel constant competition for seats, blinding the political class to legal restrictions.
Kenya needs a referendum on reducing the privileges attached to elected office and the executive

Kenya’s political governance structure also rewards loyalty and provides protection, making it easy for the elite to evade sanction. Senior government officials and politicians from across the political divide have repeatedly ignored summonses from the National Cohesion and Integration Commission, the body mandated to curb hate speech and promote inter-communal cohesion.
Such disregard for the rule of law by those in power fuels impunity and encourages political violence and early campaigning.

The Attorney General’s failure to honour the court ruling to draft legislation within the court’s deadline gives the political class leeway to keep the country in a constant state of electioneering. Police inaction against politicians who disrupt public order or make statements that undermine public trust in the electoral process compounds the problem.

To break this cycle, the Attorney General must close the legal gap by drafting the legislation the court ordered, and political parties must comply with the 2025 ruling that outlawed early campaigns. Parties should also enforce internal disciplinary measures to deter violations of the law.

Most importantly, Kenya needs a referendum on reducing the privileges attached to elected office and the executive. This could attract people motivated to serve in the executive and legislature for the public good, rather than career politicians drawn by the trappings of power. Sifuna warns opposition: deliver change in 90 days or face the streets
items.description: Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna has warned that an opposition government replacing Ruto in 2027 must deliver change within 90 days or face renewed street protests from Kenyans.
content: The Nairobi senator tells Kenyans in the United States that a post-Ruto government will have no grace period — and that the Linda Mwananchi movement will hold any successor to the same standard it holds the current administration.

Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna has warned that an opposition government replacing President William Ruto after the 2027 General Election would have no more than three months to demonstrate meaningful change before Kenyans returned to the streets, setting one of the starkest accountability benchmarks yet articulated by a senior figure in the emerging opposition coalition.

Sifuna delivered the warning during engagements with Kenyans living in the United States, where he has been meeting diaspora communities as part of efforts to build momentum for the Linda Mwananchi movement ahead of next year’s election. His message was directed as much at his own political allies as at the electorate — a deliberate signal that opposition unity, should it materialise, would carry obligations that did not expire at the ballot box.

“If we slacken, if we go there and continue with business as usual, it will not take more than three months — these young people will be back in the street saying, ‘The government must go,'” Sifuna said, referencing the Gen Z-led protests that convulsed Kenya in June 2024 and forced Ruto to withdraw the Finance Bill under sustained public pressure.

The reference was pointed and entirely intentional. Those protests — which drew tens of thousands of young Kenyans into the streets of Nairobi, Mombasa, Kisumu and beyond, resulted in approximately 62 deaths according to human rights organisations, and briefly breached the perimeter of Parliament Buildings — fundamentally altered the political landscape of Ruto’s presidency. They demonstrated, with a clarity that no opinion poll could match, that Kenya’s youth were prepared to hold governments to account through direct action when they felt that constitutional and electoral processes had failed them. Sifuna was telling his audience, and through them the opposition leadership, that the generation which brought down the Finance Bill would apply exactly the same standard to whoever succeeded Ruto.

It is a position that sets Sifuna apart from much of the opposition discourse currently circulating in Kenya’s political arena, where the conversation has concentrated heavily on the mechanics of defeating Ruto rather than on what victory would actually require in its immediate aftermath. While former Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua builds his Democracy for the Citizens Party network across the Mt Kenya region, and while various opposition figures jockey for positioning within potential coalition arrangements, Sifuna is insisting that the more urgent question is what a post-Ruto administration would do in its first quarter — and whether opposition leaders have agreed on the answer before asking Kenyans to trust them with power.

His conditions for unity are specific and economically focused. Sifuna said opposition leaders must, before forming a united political front, reach consensus on immediate measures to ease the financial burden on ordinary households. He cited reducing or eliminating taxes on fuel and electricity, and scrapping the housing levy — a mandatory deduction from payrolls that has been among the most bitterly contested elements of the Ruto administration’s fiscal policy — as priorities that any credible opposition platform must commit to delivering promptly after a change of government.

“We are not going to government to get comfortable. There will be no room for being comfortable,” Sifuna said, in remarks that carried an implicit rebuke of political cultures in which opposition movements, having secured power, rapidly accommodated themselves to the same patronage structures and spending habits they had campaigned against.

The senator argued that reducing government expenditure to create fiscal space for tax relief was not merely a policy preference but a precondition for public trust. Kenyans had, in his reading, reached a point of acute impatience with administrations that promised relief and delivered rationalisation. An opposition government that arrived in office and then began explaining why the promised changes were more complicated than anticipated would, he suggested, face a public that had heard the explanation before and was no longer prepared to accept it.

The political context surrounding Sifuna’s US trip extends beyond his remarks on accountability timelines. His engagements drew attention to a proposal, raised during a meeting with diaspora members on Saturday, that Kenyans living abroad could mobilise resources to support the construction of Jomo Kenyatta International Airport. Participant Kiemo Mohando put the idea directly: “We can build the airport. Don’t look for another Adani. We can build an airport. We can reorganise ourselves — let’s partner with the government, let’s do the airport.”

The reference to Adani placed Mohando’s proposal in an immediate and politically charged context. India’s Adani Group has featured prominently in debates about Kenya’s aviation infrastructure, and the broader controversy surrounding the conglomerate’s international operations — including bribery allegations in the United States — has made any association with Adani infrastructure projects politically sensitive in Kenya. Mohando’s suggestion that the diaspora could serve as an alternative financing source for JKIA tapped into a genuine appetite within Kenyan communities abroad to participate more directly in national development. It remained, however, a participant’s proposal rather than a formal commitment by any organised diaspora body, and Sifuna’s office did not indicate that it had been formally adopted as opposition policy.

What the exchange did illuminate is the degree to which Kenyans outside the country are engaging with the pre-election political debate with an intensity that rival the conversations happening in Nairobi’s political circles. The diaspora — concentrated in the United States, the United Kingdom, Canada and the Gulf — represents not only a source of remittances that constitute a significant portion of Kenya’s foreign exchange earnings, but an increasingly vocal constituency that opposition and government figures alike are competing to address.

For Sifuna, the US engagements served a dual purpose: reinforcing the Linda Mwananchi movement’s national reach and testing the resonance of a message built on accountability rather than simply on anti-Ruto sentiment. The distinction matters. Kenya has cycled through enough post-election disappointments to have produced a cohort of voters, particularly among the young, who are as sceptical of opposition promises as they are of government performance.

Telling that cohort that a new government would face the streets within 90 days of failing to deliver is either a remarkable act of political honesty or a carefully calibrated piece of positioning — perhaps both simultaneously. In Kenya’s pre-election landscape, the two are not always easy to distinguish.

What is clear is that the standard Sifuna has articulated publicly now follows the opposition into every conversation it has between now and August 2027. He has set the clock. The question is whether his allies are prepared to run against it.

items.title: Ruto tells Bungoma crowds the 2024 Finance Bill caused no harm
items.description: President Ruto told Bungoma crowds the 2024 Finance Bill caused no harm, blaming rivals for protests that left 62 dead and triggered a nationwide Gen Z uprising.
content: The President’s claim that Kenya’s most contested legislation passed without damage collides head-on with a documented death toll of 62 and streets that ran with teargas and blood.

President William Ruto yesterday told crowds in Bungoma County that Kenya’s 2024 Finance Bill had been passed without harming the nation, attributing the widespread protests it triggered to rival politicians who, he said, spread misinformation to manipulate young Kenyans into taking to the streets.

The remarks, delivered during a public function at which the President also disbursed sugarcane bonuses to local farmers, represent his most direct attempt yet to reframe the defining political crisis of his administration ahead of the 2027 General Election. They were also, within hours, among the most contested statements he has made since taking office — and the speed and fury of the public response suggested that the reframing had not landed as smoothly as his advisers might have hoped.

“The 2024 Finance Bill was eventually passed, and there was no harm to our nation,” Ruto told the gathering, his tone measured and confident. He then addressed the generation whose mobilisation nearly derailed his government’s fiscal agenda directly, with evident assurance: “Gen Zs wananipenda — hawatakubali kugonganishwa na Sifuna na Gachagua vile walifanya 2024.” Translated: “Gen Z loves me — they will not allow themselves to be used against me by Sifuna and Gachagua the way they were in 2024.”

The political calculation behind those words is not difficult to read. With former Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua now openly building an opposition movement through his Democracy for the Citizens Party, and Orange Democratic Movement Secretary-General Edwin Sifuna maintaining a consistent and pointed critique of the administration, Ruto is working methodically to detach Kenya’s youth from the political figures he regards as his principal threats heading into 2027. Telling Gen Z that they were manipulated rather than motivated — that their anger in 2024 was manufactured by opportunistic politicians rather than rooted in genuine grievance — is a strategy aimed at neutralising what became, in June of that year, the most significant spontaneous political mobilisation Kenya had witnessed in a generation.

The historical record, however, is not easily revised. What began as an online campaign against specific tax proposals embedded in the Finance Bill 2024 evolved, within weeks, into a nationwide movement that drew tens of thousands of young Kenyans into the streets of Nairobi, Mombasa, Kisumu, Nakuru and dozens of other towns simultaneously. On 25 June 2024, protesters breached the perimeter of Parliament Buildings in Nairobi in scenes broadcast live around the world. Security forces responded with live ammunition. By any credible account — including documentation compiled by Amnesty International Kenya and the Kenya Human Rights Commission — approximately 62 people died during the protests and their aftermath. Hundreds more were injured. Dozens were abducted in the days that followed, and a significant number remain unaccounted for.

Ruto subsequently withdrew the Finance Bill in its entirety under that sustained pressure — an extraordinary concession from a sitting president that acknowledged, implicitly and unmistakably, the potency of the opposition he faced. The withdrawal was presented by the government at the time as a demonstration of democratic responsiveness, a leader listening to his people. He later enacted a number of the bill’s revenue-raising provisions through alternative legislative and administrative mechanisms — a move that critics said achieved through the back door what had been emphatically rejected at the front. Yesterday’s remarks in Bungoma appeared to retroactively recast that entire episode as something closer to a tactical pause in the face of manufactured chaos, rather than a genuine retreat before legitimate public anger.

Social media users reacted with barely contained fury. Screenshots of teargas canisters fired directly into crowds, images of protesters bleeding on the streets outside Parliament, photographs of candlelit vigils held for those who did not come home, and carefully compiled lists of the confirmed dead circulated rapidly across X, Facebook and TikTok within hours of Ruto’s comments being broadcast nationally. For many Kenyans who had marched, who had lost friends, siblings or colleagues, or who had simply watched events unfold in real time from their phones, the suggestion that no harm had been done was not a political reframing they were willing to absorb. It was, in the words of several users whose posts gathered tens of thousands of engagements, an insult dressed as history.

The anger is entirely comprehensible. But the political logic underpinning Ruto’s approach, viewed from his own strategic position, is not irrational. The President faces a 2027 election in which the youth vote — Kenya’s largest and fastest-growing demographic bloc, with millions of first-time voters registered since the 2022 cycle — will almost certainly be decisive. If that generation can be persuaded that their 2024 mobilisation was the product of elite manipulation rather than legitimate fury at government policy, the administration neutralises one of the most powerful arguments his opponents can deploy on the campaign trail. If they cannot be persuaded, those same voters represent perhaps the most consequential electoral threat Ruto has faced since taking office.

Bungoma itself was chosen with care. The western Kenya county sits in sugarcane country, and the bonus disbursements Ruto oversaw during the same visit addressed a specific and longstanding grievance — delayed payments from millers that have damaged farming livelihoods across the region for years. That concrete delivery, money placed visibly and directly into farmers’ hands, is precisely the kind of tangible governance action the administration hopes will carry more weight with rural voters than opposition rhetoric. It is a campaign approach Ruto has deployed consistently and with some success: appear in a county, deliver a benefit, challenge opponents to match it and move on before the criticism catches up.

The Finance Bill remark overshadowed the farmer narrative entirely. By volunteering a claim so directly and so publicly contradicted by documented events — events that most Kenyans lived through, watched or participated in — Ruto handed his opponents material they were quick to deploy. Gachagua’s allies circulated the statement alongside footage of the protests within the hour. Sifuna responded publicly, calling the President’s characterisation an insult to families who had buried their children after confronting a government that had, in his telling, chosen revenue over lives.

The deeper question the episode raises concerns the nature of political truth in Kenya’s accelerating pre-election environment. With August 2027 now less than nine months away, every major public appearance by the President, every rally convened by Gachagua, every statement from the emerging opposition coalition will be examined not merely for factual accuracy but for what it signals about the narratives being tested and the alliances being assembled. In that environment, Ruto’s Bungoma remarks are less a historical claim than a campaign opening move — a deliberate declaration that he intends to contest the meaning of 2024 as vigorously as he will contest the ballot of 2027.

Whether that contest can be won depends, in substantial part, on whether the young Kenyans he addressed yesterday are prepared to accept the version of events being offered to them. The difficulty for the President is that this particular audience was not receiving information second-hand. They were there. They streamed it live. They carried the placards. They attended the funerals.
No political speech, however confident its delivery, can entirely overwrite a memory that was made in the streets, in the teargas and in the grief that followed.

items.title: Karua, Matiang’i and Nyoro take opposition message to Kirinyaga
items.description: Martha Karua, Fred Matiang'i and Ndindi Nyoro rallied Kirinyaga County residents in Kutus and Ngarubaini under the TuunganeTujikomboe banner ahead of Kenya's 2027 elections.
content: Karua, Matiang’i and Nyoro take opposition message to Kirinyaga
The Kutus rally signals a sharpening alliance as Kenya’s emerging opposition bloc tests its reach in Mt Kenya heartland.

Martha Karua, former Cabinet Secretary Fred Matiang’i and Kiharu Member of Parliament Ndindi Nyoro on Sunday took their opposition campaign to Kirinyaga County, addressing residents in Kutus and Ngarubaini in what organisers described as an overwhelmingly attended series of public engagements under the #TuunganeTujikomboe banner.

Karua, speaking after the rally, framed the gathering in deliberately measured terms, pushing back against suggestions that the emerging alliance represented political opportunism. “Democracy is built on dialogue, engagement and the willingness to find common ground,” she said. “Political alliances and partnerships are part of that process, and there is no need to mistake discussion for division.”

The trio’s appearance together in Kirinyaga — a county that sits squarely within the Mt Kenya region whose political loyalty is now fiercely contested ahead of the 2027 General Election — carries significance beyond the warm receptions reported at both venues. It represents a visible effort to plant an opposition flag in territory that President William Ruto carried convincingly in 2022.

Karua was direct about the coalition’s intended focus. “Our attention must remain firmly on the people,” she said. “Kenyans want relief from the rising cost of living, opportunities for employment, better education and accessible healthcare. They want to live with dignity and have reason to believe in tomorrow.”
The road to 2027 runs through Mt Kenya. Yesterday, three of its most prominent voices served notice they intend to contest every inch of it.

items.title: Nzoia Farmers Benefit from Sugar Mill Revival, KSh 195m Bonus Payout
items.description: Ruto issues KSh195 million in bonuses to Nzoia sugarcane farmers, part of KSh1.2 billion for western sugar belt growers, as revival creates local jobs again.
content: PAY ATTENTION: Mark TUKO.co.ke as a preferred source, and our content will appear higher in your Google feed!

Sugarcane farmers in Bungoma County are reaping the rewards of a revived Nzoia Sugar Company, with President William Ruto on Monday handing out bonus cheques worth KSh195 million to growers supplying the factory.
The event, held at the Nzoia Sugar Company grounds in Kanduyi Constituency, marked a visible milestone in the government's push to breathe new life into Kenya's struggling sugar industry.

The Bungoma payment is part of a broader KSh1.2 billion bonus distribution earmarked for farmers across the Western sugar belt, with payouts to Mumias, Chemelil, Muhoroni, Miwani and Sony sugar factory farmers set to follow.

President Ruto credited the Rai Group, the private investor that took over operations under a leasing arrangement, with rescuing a factory he said had been on the verge of collapse just three years ago.

Managing Director Tejveer Rai confirmed that the company had paid KSh1.6 billion to farmers during the year, with an additional KSh150 million channelled to cane harvesters. The firm also remitted KSh688 million in taxes to the national government and Bungoma County, alongside KSh639 million in lease and concession fees.
Ruto was clear that the leasing deal does not transfer ownership of either the factory or its nucleus estate, stressing that both assets remain the property of the people of Bungoma.

For Ferdinand Mahanu, a farmer from Tembelela Village in Mukembe Location, sugarcane growing has anchored his family's livelihood for more than 20 years, paying school fees, improving their home and covering daily needs.
He recalled how delayed payments and earnings settled in percentages under the old management had dented farmer morale and squeezed household incomes.

The arrival of improved cane varieties and consistent payment schedules has renewed his confidence in the crop. Mahanu also pointed to a ripple effect beyond the farm gate, noting that the upturn in agricultural activity is generating work for young people and women in harvesting, haulage and other parts of the supply chain.

On the broader picture, the President said national sugar output had climbed from 790,000 metric tonnes the previous year and was on track to reach 900,000 metric tonnes in 2025. The government's longer-term target stands at 1.2 million metric tonnes, the threshold it considers sufficient for the country to meet its own sugar needs.

In other news, TUKO also highlighted facts about William Ruto’s comparison of unga prices in 2022 and 2026 , including the current average cost of a 2kg packet and the government’s agricultural reforms.

Ruto said the price had fallen from KSh 230 to about KSh 152, while maize production rose and imports declined. He also cited a Nakuru farmer who increased his harvest from 75 to 125 bags on the same five acres.

items.title: NCPWD, APDK And Kilimanjaro Blind Trust Partner To Expand Accessibility And Economic Inclusion
items.description: The National Council for Persons with Disabilities (NCPWD), the Association for the Physically Disabled of Kenya (APDK) and Kilimanjaro Blind Trust Africa (K...
content: The National Council for Persons with Disabilities (NCPWD), the Association for the Physically Disabled of Kenya (APDK) and Kilimanjaro Blind Trust Africa (KBTA...

The National Council for Persons with Disabilities (NCPWD), the Association for the Physically Disabled of Kenya (APDK) and Kilimanjaro Blind Trust Africa (KBTA) have held discussions aimed at strengthening collaboration on accessibility, education, employment and economic inclusion for persons with disabilities.

The meeting brought together representatives of the three organisations, including NCPWD Chief Executive Officer Dr Michael Munene, Alex Kaluki of APDK and Sopang of KBTA. Discussions focused on identifying areas of cooperation that would improve access to assistive technology, educational opportunities and sustainable economic participation for persons with disabilities.

During the engagement, Sopang highlighted KBTA's role as a delivery partner across Kenya, Tanzania, Rwanda and Malawi, supporting children with disabilities through education, employment preparation and eye-care initiatives. The organisation works with education stakeholders, including the Ministry of Education, teacher training colleges (TTCs) and technical and vocational education and training institutions (TVETs).

KBTA presented its work across 60 Kenyan special and integrated schools, comprising 42 primary schools and 18 secondary schools. Its interventions include providing assistive technologies, accessible learning materials and technical support to improve the participation of visually impaired learners in mainstream and special education institutions.

Among the technologies highlighted was the Orbit Reader 20, a portable refreshable Braille display that enables visually impaired learners to read and write digital content independently. The device has a 20-cell Braille display and supports access to electronic educational materials, helping learners participate more effectively in classroom activities.

Another technology showcased was the Orion TI-84 Plus talking scientific graphing calculator, designed to help visually impaired students access mathematical and scientific concepts. According to the meeting account, the initiative is currently benefiting approximately 1,500 students, with teachers also receiving training in equipment maintenance and repairs to support continued use.

items.title: Bayern vs Ajax match set to unlock business opportunities for Kenyan SMEs
items.description: A full stadium creates demand far beyond its gates. Tony Lungaho has named the sectors that stand to gain from Talanta's opening day. Here is what 5 January
content: Visitors who fly in for a match rarely fly straight out. Lungaho has pointed to Kenya's attractions, from the Mara to the beaches
A full stadium creates demand far beyond its gates. Tony Lungaho has named the sectors that stand to gain from Talanta’s opening day. Here is what 5 January could mean for each.

When FC Bayern Munich and AFC Ajax open the Raila Odinga International Stadium at Talanta Sports City on 5 January, the turnstiles will not be the only place money changes hands. Tony Lungaho, CEO of the AFCON PAMOJA 2027 Local Organising Committee, highlights that hotels, transport, restaurants, retail, tourism operators and local suppliers, as well as media, technology and creative businesses.

Not every fan is local. Almost 10 per cent of tickets sold so far went to buyers outside Kenya, Lungaho says, from as far as Kazakhstan and Colombia. The two clubs have also asked for 5,000 tickets for their travelling supporters. Every one of those visitors needs a bed.
With gates opening at 11:00 and an evening kick-off, 5 January is a full day out. Expect fans to meet for a meal on the way in and to keep celebrating, or commiserating, long after the final whistle.
Getting a stadium crowd to Ngong Road and home again is a business in itself. Routes and road closures will come from the responsible agencies, so operators should watch for their notices.

A food festival is part of the programme. With no re-entry for this match, fans inside will be eating and drinking there for the day. Details of the vendors will be announced through official channels.
Sound and staging crews, lighting technicians, security and cleaning firms, stewards and ticket scanners: a stadium opening with a concert attached needs all of them.
Bayern Munich vs Ajax: Ticket prices, how to buy and stadium entry rules

Lungaho has described an A-list concert as part of the day, and he hints at a line-up of around 15 local and international artists. He sees Talanta as a home for concerts and live entertainment, part of Kenya’s creative economy. Behind every act is a team: DJs, dancers, stylists, photographers, videographers and content creators.
Bayern and Ajax have almost half a billion followers between them, Lungaho says, and both have loyal supporters’ groups in Kenya. Expect demand for jerseys, scarves and anything in team colours.

Visitors who fly in for a match rarely fly straight out. Lungaho has pointed to Kenya’s attractions, from the Mara to the beaches, as part of the pitch for sports tourism, and the LOC is targeting at least 500,000 international visitors between January and July 2027. His summary of the ambition: “If we make it possible, the world will come to Africa.”

One match will not transform Nairobi’s economy on its own. But as a first test of whether a Kenyan stadium can pull in visitors, spending and repeat events, 5 January matters, and AFCON PAMOJA 2027 follows from 19 June to 17 July.

Kenya’s Gambling Regulation: Six Regulations, One Uncertain Future
items.description: Kenya’s six new gambling regulations aim for credible oversight, but licensing costs and capital requirements spark investor concern.
content: Kenya’s ambitious gambling regulatory overhaul promises stronger oversight, improved consumer protection and a more structured investment environment. However, six new regulatory instruments have triggered industry opposition, parliamentary scrutiny and legal challenges over licensing fees, capital requirements and market access.

As operators and investors reassess the cost of doing business, the bigger question is whether Kenya is building a more credible gambling economy or creating regulatory barriers that could undermine its commercial ambitions.

Kenya wants a more disciplined gambling industry. That ambition is legitimate. An industry generating commercial activity, attracting international operators and increasingly migrating towards digital platforms cannot operate effectively without strong regulatory oversight.

However, there is a difference between regulating a market and making participation in that market prohibitively expensive. The introduction of six Gambling Control Regulations in 2026 has exposed precisely this dilemma. Rather than receiving an uncomplicated welcome, the regulatory overhaul has generated objections from industry stakeholders, judicial challenges and parliamentary scrutiny.

Investors are watching. They want predictable licensing, proportionate compliance costs, enforceable rules and confidence that regulatory decisions will not undermine the value of their investments. Kenya must understand that regulatory credibility is not measured by the number of regulations introduced but by the quality, consistency and economic consequences of their implementation.

Developed under the Gambling Control Act, 2025, the six statutory instruments constitute an integrated framework covering market entry, operational conduct, advertising, foreign-based operators, the National Lottery and dispute resolution.

The Licensing Regulations establish requirements for operators, including bookmakers, casinos, lotteries and other gambling businesses. They determine application procedures, eligibility, fees and minimum capital requirements.
The Conduct of Gambling Operations Regulations establish operational standards, including financial controls, customer protection, internal management and compliance obligations.

The Advertising Regulations address the promotion of gambling products, including marketing practices and consumer protection. Their implementations will influence how operators acquire customers and communicate with the market.
The National Lottery Regulations provide the framework for administering Kenya’s national lottery and directing its proceeds towards designated public-benefit objectives
The Foreign-based Operators Regulations seek to bring cross-border gambling businesses serving relevant markets within Kenya’s regulatory perimeter.
Finally, the Gambling Appeals Tribunal Regulations establish procedures for challenging regulatory decisions and resolving disputes.

Collectively, these instruments represent a significant attempt to modernize Kenya’s gambling architecture. The problem is not ambition. It is whether their requirements are proportionate, legally sound and economically workable.
The licensing controversy: The price of doing business legally

Nothing illustrates the controversy more clearly than the licensing requirements. Under the reported gazette fee structure, an online bookmaker faces an application fee of KSH5 million, a license fee of KSH50 million and an annual operating fee of KSH5 million. Its minimum gambling capital requirement is KSh100 million. These are separate financial obligations. The capital requirement should not be mistaken for a government fee: it represents money the operator must demonstrate as qualifying capital. Nevertheless, the combined financial commitment is substantial.

Consider the difference between an established international operator with considerable financial resources and a smaller Kenyan business attempting to enter the market. Both face regulatory obligations but their ability to absorb licensing costs, technology investment, legal expenses and compliance expenditure is fundamentally different. The government’s own regulatory impact Statement acknowledges that small and medium-sized operators face high compliance compared with a moderate burden for large operators. It also identifies increased market concentration as a potential consequence. This is not an argument against financial requirements. Regulators must ensure that operators possess sufficient resources to meet their obligations and protect customers.

However, capital requirements must be supported by transparent economic reasonings. A licensing structure that excludes legitimate businesses without demonstratly I,proving consumer protection risks becoming a barrier to competition. Kenya must explain how it arrived at these figures and whether the costs reflect the actual requirements of effective regulation.
Parliament, the Courts and the question of legality

The controversy has moved beyond industry complaints. On 28 July 2026, the six statutory instruments were tabled in the in the Senate. The Association of Gaming Operators-Kenya raised concerns about the regulations, including licensing costs, minimum capital requirements, stakeholders’ consultation and alleged procedural and legal inconsistencies. The Senate subsequently extended the committee’s consideration period by 21 days, setting 26 November 2026 as the deadline for concluding its review.

Meanwhile, the High Court has been considering challenges to the licensing framework. In Judicial Review E251 of 2026, the applicants challenged the Licensing Regulations. On 7 August, the court limited its interim stay to the increased fees and the gambling capital requirements. The Gambling Regulatory Authority subsequently argued that the suspension was preventing it from processing applications. It told the court that 246 applications were pending. On 21 August, the court allowed implementation of the licensing framework and collection of the contested fees pending determination of the substantive dispute, subject to the regulator’s undertaking to refund fees if ultimately found unlawful.
That decision did not establish that the disputed fees were lawful. It allowed their implementation while the substantive challenge remained unresolved. This distinction matters enormously.
Parliamentary scrutiny and judicial proceedings are separate processes. Neither should be presented as an automatic annulment of the regulations.

For investors, however, the existence of unresolved legal questions is itself a commercial concern. Businesses cannot confidently calculate long-term returns when the financial conditions governing market entry remain contested.
The commercial consequences: Who wins and who loses?

The first potential winners are established operators with significant capital, technology and compliance infrastructure to absorb the additional requirements. Smaller businesses may face a different reality: acquisition, consolidation, restructuring or withdrawal. This could create opportunities for investors seeking to acquire existing operators. However, acquisition involving contested licenses and uncertain regulatory obligations require particularly careful due diligence.

Advertising restrictions also have commercial consequences. Operators may need to redesign promotional campaigns, reconsider sponsorship arrangements and invest in alternative customer acquisition strategies.

Technology companies, meanwhile, could benefit from increased demand for identity verification, anti-money laundering systems, cybersecurity, transaction monitoring and responsible gambling solutions.

There is another danger. If the legal market becomes excessively expensive while unlicensed platforms remain accessible, consumers and operators may migrate towards less regulated alternatives. The government’s own impact assessment recognizes this possibility. Regulation that increases compliance without strengthening enforcement risks rewarding precisely the businesses it is intended to control.
The investor equation: Opportunity versus regulatory risk

For international investors, Kenya remains commercially interesting. Its established betting culture, digital infrastructure and regional business relevance offer opportunities across gambling, payments and technology. However, market potential are not the same as investment certainty. The immediate implications are higher entry costs, greater regulatory due diligence, potentially increased cost of capital and uncertainty surrounding licensing decisions. Private equity investors must examine license validity, ownership structures, outstanding regulatory obligations and litigation exposure before acquiring operators.
Local entrepreneurs face the possibility that financial thresholds will restrict their ability to compete.
Technology investors may find opportunities in compliance infrastructure, monitoring systems and consumer protection solutions.

International operators must also evaluate the implications of foreign-based operator requirements and the cost of establishing a complaint market presence. The opportunity is not disappearing. It is becoming more selective.

Investors will favor jurisdictions where regulatory obligations are transparent, consistently enforced and proportionate to commercial realities. Kenya must recognize that capital is mobile. Investors can redirect resources towards markets offering a better balance between opportunity and risk. Kenya needs proportionate licensing fees, transparent capital requirements and predictable renewal procedures. It must strengthen enforcement against illegal operators rather than place the entire compliance burden in legitimate businesses.

The appeals mechanism must command confidence, The National Lottery must operate with transparent governance and advertising restrictions must protect consumers without creating arbitrary commercial disadvantages.

Moat importantly, player protection must be measurable. The success of regulation should be assessed through improvements in age verification, self-exclusion, responsible gambling interventions, complaint resolution and enforcement against illegal operators.
Conclusion: Regulation must create confidence not just control

Kenya has an opportunity to establish one of Africa’s most credible gambling regulatory environments but ambition alone will not achieve it. Six regulations can create an impressive legal architecture. They cannot by themselves guarantee investment, competition or consumer protection. The real test is whether Kenya can reconcile government oversight with commercial sustainability. A market that is expensive to enter, uncertain to operate and difficult to predict is not necessarily a well-regulated market. It may simply be an expansive market.

Investors do not demand freedom from regulation. They demand regulation they can understand, price and trust. Kenya must decide whether it wants to regulate gambling out of existence or build an industry in which responsible operators, consumers, government and investors can all have a sustainable stake.
That is the future its six regulations must justify.

items.description: Kenya’s National Treasury disputes claims foreign debt rose KSh 233.4bn, saying just KSh 95.7bn was disbursed and the rest reflects future loan commitments.

The National Treasury has formally disputed a Daily Nation report that Kenya's foreign debt increased by KSh 233.4 billion over four months, arguing that the figure refers to signed loan agreements rather than money the government actually received.
Cabinet Secretary John Mbadi signed the rejoinder on November 23, 2026, the same day the newspaper published its article titled "Foreign debt up by Sh233bn in 4 months."
The report had drawn on the Treasury's statutory submission to Parliament covering external loans contracted between May 1 and August 31, 2026.

At the core of the Treasury's objection is the distinction between contracted loans and actual debt.

Of the seven loan agreements signed during the reporting period, only two had been disbursed by the time the report reached Parliament: KSh 44.1 billion from the World Bank's International Bank for Reconstruction and Development and KSh 51.6 billion from the International Development Association, bringing total disbursements to KSh 95.7 billion.
The remaining KSh 137.7 billion had not yet been released and could be drawn down progressively over several years depending on project conditions.
It further noted that Kenya repaid KSh 89.97 billion in maturing external loans during the same four-month window.
The Treasury also took issue with the description of the lenders.

Of the seven agreements, six were with multilateral development institutions, specifically the World Bank Group and the African Development Bank, while the seventh was a bilateral concessional loan from the Kingdom of Denmark.

It highlighted that KSh 132.9 billion, approximately 57% of the total, came from the International Development Association, which it described as one of the most concessional sources of development financing available globally.
Those loans carry an annual interest rate of 1.5%, include a grace period of roughly five years before principal repayments begin, and extend to repayment schedules running to 2050 and 2051.

On the broader debt trajectory, the Treasury noted that public debt denominated in foreign currencies dropped from 47.0% to 44.6% between June 2025 and June 2026, while the average time to maturity of total public debt extended from 8.3 years to 8.5 years.
Multilateral creditors now account for 55.3% of the external debt portfolio.

The proposed fund would finance home purchases, construction, renovations, residential land acquisition, property equity release and personal vehicle purchases, with repayments recycled to support new borrowers.
However, the scheme would exclusively benefit TSC Secretariat staff and would not cover the hundreds of thousands of teachers employed by the Commission.

Members of the public can submit written comments by 5:00 p.m. on December 8, 2026, while an in-person consultation meeting is scheduled for December 1 at the Kenyatta International Convention Centre in Nairobi.

The Kenya Revenue Authority (KRA) has designated official channels through which taxpayers can submit applications for the review of tax decisions, covering both customs and domestic tax disputes.

The authority issued two separate public notices under the Commissioner for Legal and Board Services, citing Section 229 of the East African Community Customs Management Act, 2004, as well as Section 73 of the Tax Procedures Act (Cap. 469B), as the legal basis for the designations.

Taxpayers aggrieved by decisions of the Commissioner of Customs and Border Control, as well as those disputing rulings by the Commissioner of Large Taxpayers or the Commissioner of Micro and Small Taxpayers, may now serve their documents through two routes.

The customs appeals designation applies to persons aggrieved by a decision of the Commissioner of Customs and Border Control and covers applications for review under Gazette Notice No. 1036 of 2019, which delegates relevant powers to the Legal and Board Services Department.

items.title: “Outlets at risk”: Stakeholders warn alcohol bill could cost Kenya KSh 8.46bn
items.description: Kenyan hospitality, labour and transport stakeholders warn the 2026 alcohol control Bill threatens 30,000 jobs and costs KSh 8.46 billion as they urge revisions.
content: PAY ATTENTION: Mark TUKO.co.ke as a preferred source, and our content will appear higher in your Google feed!
Amos Khaemba is a Current Affairs Editor at TUKO.co.ke, covering general news. Khaemba has over four years of journalism experience and joined TUKO.co.ke in 2022.

Nairobi - Stakeholders from Kenya's hospitality, entertainment , labour and transport sectors have sounded the alarm over the proposed Alcoholic Drinks and Drug Control Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026, warning that several of its provisions could destroy tens of thousands of jobs and drive consumers towards illicit alcohol.

The Bill, published in the Kenya Gazette Supplement on September 18, 2026, proposes raising the legal drinking age from 18 to 21 years, banning alcohol sales in restaurants and certain hospitality establishments, and introducing transport restrictions that critics say would penalise motorcycle riders who earn a living moving licensed goods.
William Ruto says gov’t passed 2024 Finance Bill that resulted in 62 deaths: “Caused no harm”

Michael Kiragu Muthami, Chairman of the Pubs, Entertainment, Restaurants Association of Kenya (PERAK), said the proposed amendments could force roughly 10,000 outlets to shut down, putting approximately 30,000 direct jobs at risk and generating an estimated annual economic loss of KSh 8.46 billion.

He rejected the proposed drinking age increase outright.
He also challenged the rationale for barring restaurants from holding alcohol licences, asking: "Which restaurant can you go to and not be served?"
Sava Wycliffe, Secretary-General of the Kenya Hotels and Allied Workers Union (KHAWU), echoed those concerns, warning that raising the drinking age would trigger redundancies across the sector.

Wycliffe called on Parliament to delete the clause restricting alcohol sales in hospitality establishments and replace it with targeted safeguards focused on responsible service and compliance.

Boda boda operators also pushed back against provisions that would restrict the transportation of alcoholic drinks between 6am and 6pm, with Kenya Riders and Owners Bodaboda Sacco Chairman Elly Kegode warning that motorcycle riders depend on distribution work for their income. He also challenged a proposed KSh 10 million fine or imprisonment for those found transporting alcohol.

Student representative MalcomX from Multimedia University raised a different dimension, arguing that raising the drinking age to 21 could block younger students in hospitality courses from accessing industrial attachments and jobs. He also cautioned that tightening formal access without addressing demand could push young people towards illicit products.
All stakeholders said they support eliminating illicit alcohol and protecting minors, but urged Parliament to craft regulations that strengthen the formal sector rather than undermine it.

items.title: Inside proposed route, stations, and design of Naivasha-Kisumu-Malaba SGR
items.description: Kenya Railways plans a 263.77-kilometre rail extension featuring 25 stations, 15 bridges, eight tunnels, and a new Kisumu Port.
content: Plans to extend Kenya's Standard Gauge Railway from Naivasha to Kisumu and onward to Malaba detail a major rail corridor across western Kenya. The proposed expansion follows earlier ground-breaking efforts by Kenya Railways and arrives alongside ongoing roadworks on the Rironi-Mau Summit corridor.

According to technical specifications released by Kenya Railways, the main railway line will span 263.77 kilometres. The alignment will connect key counties and towns, establishing a continuous rail link from the Rift Valley to the Ugandan border. Within Narok County alone, the track will cover approximately 94.1 kilometres before advancing through Bomet, Sotik, Sondu, and Ahero into Kisumu County.

Civil engineering works along the route include 15 railway bridges with a combined length of 43 kilometres. Engineers also plan to bore eight tunnels spanning 13.863 kilometres in total to navigate the region's varied terrain. Drainage infrastructure will require 460 culverts covering nine kilometres along the corridor.

Land acquisition and right-of-way parameters have been defined for the entire stretch. The railway corridor will measure 70 metres wide along the main line, expanding to 100 metres within designated station areas. Kenya Railways has mapped out 25 stations across the network, comprising one major station, six intermediate stations, and 18 crossing stations to manage train traffic.

Beyond the main track, the blueprint includes an 8.9-kilometre branch line connecting directly to Kisumu Port. This spur will incorporate one bridge and eight culverts. Crucially, the broader project scope encompasses constructing a new port facility in Kisumu to expand cargo handling capacity on Lake Victoria.

Kenya's existing SGR network currently terminates at Suswa in Narok County, following the completion of Phase 1 from Mombasa to Nairobi and Phase 2A from Nairobi to Naivasha. Extending the track to Malaba completes the Kenyan section of the Northern Corridor rail master plan, linking the port of Mombasa directly to landlocked neighbours in East Africa.

Project documentation outlines several economic and logistical objectives tied to the railway extension. Planners expect the line to strengthen the regional integrated transportation network and improve cross-border connectivity. Lower freight transit times and improved passenger mobility are projected to stimulate regional and national economic growth.

Additional projected outcomes include supporting tourism and creating construction and operational employment for local communities along the route. In Kisumu, the upgraded port infrastructure is intended to support blue economy activities around Lake Victoria. Information regarding the proposed project specifications and design was originally reported by People Daily.

Null and void: Court declares 2% deduction from SHA claims unconstitutional
items.description: Justice Reuben Nyakundi delivered the virtual ruling on Tuesday, November 24, 2026, finding that the government had not properly consulted Kenyans.
content: PAY ATTENTION: TUKO is in WhatsApp Channels now! Subscribe and read news in your favourite messenger.

The High Court in Vihiga has declared the 2% Health Information Management Service (HIMS) charge levied on healthcare facilities processing claims through the Social Health Authority (SHA) unconstitutional, citing a failure to adequately involve the public before the deduction was introduced.

Justice Reuben Nyakundi delivered the virtual ruling on Tuesday, November 24, 2026, finding that while the law empowers the Digital Health Agency (DHA) to collect fees for services it provides, the government had not demonstrated that Kenyans were specifically consulted on the 2% rate, the maximum deduction ceiling, or the methodology used to arrive at it.
Governors reject Health PS Oluga’s order to remove paybill numbers from county hospitals
Search option is now available at TUKO! Feel free to search the content on topics/people you enjoy reading about in the top right corner ;)

The charge, provided for under Regulation 11(2) and the Third Schedule of the Digital Health (Data Exchange Component) Regulations, 2025, requires healthcare facilities to remit 2% of approved claims, with a cap of KSh 5,000 per claim.

The court acknowledged that Section 48(1)(c) of the Digital Health Act, 2023, grants the DHA authority to charge for its services, but held that this statutory basis does not exempt the government from meeting constitutional obligations when fixing the actual amount.

The provision was found to contravene Articles 10(2)(a) and 201(a) of the Constitution, which require public participation in governance and openness in public finance, as well as Section 5 of the Statutory Instruments Act.
Kenyan moves to court to overturn Cheptumo Ayabei's TSC CEO appointment, cites irregularities

Justice Nyakundi also questioned whether the government had sufficiently explained the rationale behind settling on 2% and how the funds collected relate to the actual costs of running the digital health infrastructure. The court found that evidence of stakeholder engagements and public notices submitted by the government did not demonstrate meaningful engagement on the specific percentage-based deduction.

Despite declaring the charge unconstitutional, the court did not immediately nullify it. It suspended the declaration of invalidity for 120 days, giving the government a window to address the identified defects through a lawful process, thereby avoiding disruption to healthcare facilities and SHA claim processing during that period.

The court rejected the petitioners' request that the government reimburse healthcare providers for past deductions, noting that the fees had been collected under a published regulatory instrument in connection with services actually rendered.

The petition was filed by Dr Magare Gikenyi Benjamin, Eliud Karanja Matindi and Busia Senator Okiya Omtatah, who challenged the legality, implementation and financial accountability of the HIMS utilisation fee. In August 2026, the court had declined to suspend the deductions at the interim stage after the petitioners' application was found to lack a properly filed supporting affidavit.

Health Cabinet Secretary Aden Duale had previously defended the charge, maintaining it was legally provided for, capped at KSh 5,000 per transaction, and intended to support Kenya's digital health infrastructure.

items.description: In a bid to enhance adequate preparations for the 2027 World Athletics Championships in Beijing, China, Athletics Kenya has expanded its track and field meets by adding two series to its calendar.
content: In a bid to enhance adequate preparations for the 2027 World Athletics Championships in Beijing, China, Athletics Kenya has expanded its track and field meets by adding two series to its calendar.
Next year’s World Athletics Championships will be staged in China from 11th to 19th September.
AK’s 2027 track and field weekend meetings will now comprise 8 series, with the 1st Track and Field Weekend Meet scheduled for 8th and 9th January 2027 at the Nyayo National Stadium in Nairobi.
The 2nd Track and Field Weekend Meet will be held on 5th and 6th February 2027, also at the Nyayo National Stadium, followed by the third series in Mbaraki, in Mombasa County, between 5th–6th March.
Action will then return to Nairobi at the Ulinzi Sports Complex for the fourth meet from 2nd to 3rd April, followed by the Kamariny series in Iten town between 16th and 17th April.
Siaya County will host the 6th leg on 23rd and 24th April, followed by the 7th meet at Afraha Stadium in Nakuru County from 7th to 8th May 2027.
The season will conclude with the 8th meet scheduled for 21st to 22nd May at the Ulinzi Sports Complex.

Athletics Kenya has called on athletes to familiarise themselves with the World Athletics qualification system and entry standards and take advantage of the available competition opportunities to achieve the required qualifying marks for Beijing World Athletics Championships.

Athletics Kenya President Jack Tuwei Asks Doping Offenders 'Why Do It?' After 'Shameful Week' for Kenyan Athletics
items.description: NAIROBI, Kenya — Athletics Kenya president Jack Tuwei has confronted the country's doping offenders head-on, asking cheats "Why do it?" after a "shameful week" in which fresh doping offences again damaged the standing…
content: NAIROBI, Kenya — Athletics Kenya president Jack Tuwei has confronted the country's doping offenders head-on, asking cheats "Why do it?" after a "shameful week" in which fresh doping offences again damaged the standing of the world's most celebrated distance-running nation.

In remarks reported by Nairobi-based broadcaster Capital FM, Tuwei took aim at elite athletes who engage in doping offences, saying their conduct soils the image of a country whose runners have carried its flag onto podium after podium for decades. His intervention came after a week in which Kenyan athletics was rocked by new doping cases, the latest chapter in a crisis that has shadowed the East African athletics superpower for more than a decade.

Kenya's dominance is what gives the crisis its sting. Kenyan athletes routinely collect titles at the Olympic Games, the World Athletics Championships and the six World Marathon Majors in Boston, London, Berlin, Chicago, New York and Tokyo, and the country's distance-running pipeline is studied and emulated around the world. That success has also made Kenyan athletes one of the most heavily tested populations in global track and field.

The Athletics Integrity Unit, the anti-doping arm of World Athletics, has for years recorded Kenyan athletes among the largest national groups in its caseload, with dozens of runners suspended over the past decade, a large share of them road-running specialists. Each new cluster of cases revives scrutiny of whether the country's testing, education and intelligence systems are keeping pace with its talent production.

Those stakes are written into the sport's rulebook. World Athletics classifies Kenya in Category A, its strictest anti-doping tier, under which athletes from listed federations must undergo at least three no-notice, out-of-competition tests in the ten months before a World Championships or Olympic Games simply to be eligible to compete. The classification ties Kenya's participation at major championships directly to the conduct of its athletes and the rigour of its domestic testing regime.

Kenya has built a legal and institutional framework in response. The Anti-Doping Act of 2016 criminalised doping after the country was briefly declared non-compliant by the World Anti-Doping Agency, and the Anti-Doping Agency of Kenya, known as ADAK, conducts domestic testing and athlete education. In late 2022 the Kenyan government pledged 25 million US dollars over five years to strengthen anti-doping programmes, one of the largest financial commitments of its kind by any athletics nation.

The alternative to reform has been demonstrated elsewhere in the sport. World Athletics barred Russia's federation from international competition for years after uncovering state-sponsored doping, a precedent regularly cited whenever debate over Kenya's case numbers intensifies. Athletics Kenya has previously endorsed sanctions against its own athletes and worked alongside the Athletics Integrity Unit, while Tuwei's latest remarks place responsibility squarely on competitors who choose to cheat despite the rewards available to clean runners.

The question of whether the message is landing will be tested at the highest level, with the 2027 World Athletics Championships scheduled for Beijing, where Category A testing requirements will once again govern the eligibility of Kenyan athletes. Sanctions for international-level athletes rest with the Athletics Integrity Unit, which publishes disciplinary rulings as cases move through its process.

items.title: US pact advances Kenya's nuclear energy ambitions
items.description: A Kenyan delegation met American officials in Washington to begin formal negotiations on a bilateral civil nuclear cooperation agreement.
content: Between 16 and 20 November, Justus Wabuyabo, Chief Executive Officer of the Nuclear Power and Energy Agency (NuPEA), led a multi-agency delegation to Washington, D.C.

The team met at the Harry S. Truman Building to start formal negotiations on a Section 123 Agreement between Kenya and the United States. This bilateral framework governs the transfer of civil nuclear material, equipment and technical expertise under the US Atomic Energy Act.

Signing a Section 123 Agreement is a legal prerequisite for any country seeking to acquire American nuclear reactor technology or fuel services. Without the pact, US companies cannot legally export major nuclear components to Kenyan energy developers.

NuPEA is the state corporation mandated to promote and implement Kenya's nuclear electricity programme. The agency coordinates feasibility studies, site selection and regulatory frameworks required before physical plant construction can begin.

Negotiating with Washington aligns with Kenya's long-term infrastructure planning to diversify its national electricity grid. While the country relies heavily on geothermal, hydro and wind resources, planners have earmarked nuclear generation to provide stable baseload power for industrial growth.

The Washington talks involved officials from multiple Kenyan government institutions. Technical discussions during such negotiations typically cover non-proliferation commitments, physical security standards and environmental safeguards.

Wabuyabo noted that the November meetings marked the formal start of these treaty discussions with American counterparts. Both governments must review and ratify the final text before commercial technology transfers can proceed.

Kenya has spent over a decade developing institutional capacity through partnerships with the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA). Training local engineers, drafting radiation protection laws and assessing coastal and inland sites remain ongoing priorities for NuPEA.
The original commentary detailing the Washington delegation was authored by Justus Wabuyabo and published by Business Daily Africa on 23 November 2026.
