Itel Energy Launches Portable Power Stations In Kenya As Demand For Backup Energy Grows
items.description: China’s Itel Energy has launched its solar and battery storage business in Kenya, unveiling two portable power stations as it seeks to expand in a market
content: China’s Itel Energy has launched its solar and battery storage business in Kenya, unveiling two portable power stations as it seeks to expand in a market where households and businesses are looking for alternatives to grid electricity during outages.
Wang Zhuoyu, Itel Energy’s Kenya country manager, said the company’s expansion was part of a broader strategy to develop renewable energy and integrated power solutions for emerging markets.

“Our focus is on creating sustainable growth and developing products that address the specific needs of different markets and industries,” she said. “We believe our experience across multiple markets gives us a better understanding of customers and the challenges they face.”
Wang said Itel Energy had taken about two years to become the market leader in Nigeria, an achievement he attributed to its distribution network and product quality.

“It took us approximately two years of sustained effort to become the market leader in Nigeria,” she said. “That achievement is particularly important to us because it reflects two critical aspects of our business: the strength of our distribution network and the quality and sustainability of our products.”

Itel Energy entered the Kenyan market last month and said it had a presence in over 20 countries, eleven of them in Africa. The company said it was also a leading solar energy solutions provider in Pakistan. The launch in Kenya is also intended to open the Somalia and South Sudan markets.

The company distributes hybrid and on-grid inverters, batteries, all-in-one systems, energy storage cabinets and photovoltaic modules. It has seven official service centres in Nairobi, Mombasa, Kiambu, Nakuru, Meru, Uasin Gishu and Kisumu counties, and more than 100 distributors in over 20 towns.

The two portable power stations target different levels of electricity demand. The Power Go is designed for smaller electronic devices, including smartphones, laptops, Wi-Fi routers, LED lights and CCTV cameras.

Its 100,000 mAh battery could keep a household internet router running for several hours or provide backup power for a laptop, depending on the equipment’s consumption and energy losses. Its compact design is aimed at students, remote workers and households needing portable power for essential electronics.
The Power Tank has a 1kWh battery and a nominal AC output of 500 watts, allowing it to operate selected household appliances such as televisions, fans, routers, laptops and LED lighting.

A household could run several of these devices simultaneously, provided their combined electricity demand remains below the system’s output limit. Actual operating time would depend on the appliances connected and their power consumption.

The unit is not designed for high-consumption appliances such as electric kettles, microwaves, irons and cooking equipment, which typically require more than 500W. Refrigerators would also need careful assessment because compressor startup can draw more power than normal operation.

Both products support solar charging. The Power Go accepts solar input of up to 100W, while the Power Tank supports up to 400W, allowing users with compatible panels to recharge the batteries without relying entirely on the electricity grid. The cost and availability of solar panels could, however, increase the initial investment.

Itel Energy’s pricing places the products in a competitive market. EcoFlow’s River 2, which has a 256Wh battery and 300W AC output, has been advertised in Kenya at about Sh26,650, while the River 3, with 245Wh of storage and a 300W output, has been listed at approximately Sh31,370.Bluetti’s Premium 30 V2, with a 320Wh battery and 600W AC output, has been advertised at around Sh34,000.
In the 1kWh category, a comparable YACHU model has been listed at approximately Sh45,000, while EcoFlow’s E980, with 980Wh of storage and a 500W output, has been advertised at around Sh62,380.

Portable battery systems are increasingly marketed as alternatives to petrol generators and fixed inverter installations. Their portability and ability to store solar energy appeal to consumers seeking to keep communications equipment and essential appliances running, although their limited battery capacity and power output mean they cannot replace a full household electricity supply.
One of the Itel Energy partners in Kenya, said the company was working with local partners to develop solar installations in shopping malls and other commercial facilities.
“Together with Itel Energy, we aim to advance solar and battery technology with local market knowledge, professional installation and dependable technical support,” he said.

He said Kenya’s electricity infrastructure could benefit from hybrid energy systems combining solar generation, battery storage and energy management technology, but added that the initial cost remained a barrier for many businesses.

“We recognise that the initial investment remains a challenge for many businesses,” he said. “That is why affordable financing is important. We must work towards making these solutions accessible to more customers.”
Ali said the company’s intention was to complement existing electricity providers rather than compete with Kenya Power, the country’s main electricity distributor.
“Our intention is not to compete with Kenya Power but to work alongside existing electricity providers and complement the national grid,” he said.
Joseph Mwaniki, local service manager, said the company would provide after-sales support to customers using Itel Energy products.

“We will offer all the support the customers may require in after sales,” he said. “In case of any challenges on the Itel Energy products, we request customers to reach out to us through 070969888. They can visit the nearest Calcare office near them because we are present all over Kenya.”
Wang said the company’s longer-term objective was to build a business focused on sustainability and the changing energy needs of customers.

“We want to create opportunities for future generations and build a business founded on respect, sustainability and long-term value,” she said. “Our transition towards renewable energy and integrated energy solutions is part of a broader commitment to supporting Africa and other emerging markets.”

items.title: AI is making Kenyan students faster — but are they thinking better?
items.description: AI tools are reshaping learning across Kenya's schools and TVET colleges, but educators warn the system must prioritise critical thinking over faster access to answers
content: Generative tools are reshaping classrooms from Nairobi to rural TVET colleges, but educators warn that speed without judgement is not learning.

Artificial intelligence is changing how Kenyan students learn, but the education system’s most pressing challenge is ensuring that faster access to information translates into deeper understanding rather than a sophisticated shortcut to the same shallow thinking it has always struggled to address.

From secondary schools and universities to TVET institutions and professional training programmes, learners across Kenya can now use AI tools to summarise notes, explain difficult concepts, generate essay structures and produce written work in seconds. The opportunity is real and significant. So is the risk of mistaking the speed of an answer for the quality of the thinking behind it.

The question facing Kenya’s education institutions is no longer whether students will use AI. Many already do, quietly and routinely, in ways that range from entirely legitimate to academically dishonest. What matters now is whether they are being taught to use it with judgement — and whether the system is measuring the right things.

Verification must come first. Generative AI produces confident, well-structured responses that can be incomplete, outdated or factually wrong. A student researching Kenya’s economic policy, climate record, constitutional history or public health data cannot assume that a fluent paragraph is an accurate one. Learners need to compare sources, check publication dates, interrogate claims and develop an instinct for where information originates and who benefits from its framing.

This reality makes critical thinking more valuable, not less. For much of Kenya’s education history, students were rewarded for locating and reproducing information — the right answer in the right place at the right time. In an AI-enabled learning environment, the more important skill is assessing whether information is credible, relevant and applicable to a specific problem, and then doing something useful with it. That is a harder skill to teach and a harder one to examine, but it is the one that will determine how well a graduate functions in a workplace where AI is already embedded.

Privacy requires clearer and earlier guidance than most institutions are currently providing. Students should understand that personal data, confidential school records and sensitive information should not be entered into public AI platforms without consideration of where that data goes and how it is stored. As Kenya continues to build its data protection culture under the Data Protection Act and the oversight of the Office of the Data Protection Commissioner, responsible technology use must become part of digital literacy from an early age.

The plagiarism question demands a more considered institutional response than outright prohibition. Banning AI tools is difficult to enforce, often counterproductive and can obscure the larger pedagogical point. Education should measure whether a learner understands a subject, can defend a position under questioning and can apply knowledge to unfamiliar problems. That demands a greater emphasis on oral presentations, classroom discussions, practical assignments and project-based assessments — formats in which AI assistance is visible and the student’s own thinking is unavoidable.

Prompting is itself becoming a teachable and genuinely useful skill. A learner who can frame a precise question, provide sufficient context, refine an instruction and critically evaluate the response is developing capabilities that employers across sectors are beginning to actively seek. But prompting should sharpen thinking, not replace it. The student who accepts the first output without interrogation has not learned to use AI — they have learned to defer to it.

Parents and teachers carry responsibilities that go beyond policing tool use. The more productive questions are not whether a student used AI, but how they verified the answer, what they learned in the process, what they would challenge in the output and whether they can explain the idea without the tool in front of them. Those questions shift the focus from enforcement to education, which is where it belongs.

These capabilities will matter well beyond any examination hall. As AI integrates further into Kenya’s workplaces, employers will need people who can assess AI-generated information with scepticism, identify errors, exercise independent judgement and apply knowledge to problems that do not have pre-generated answers. Using AI fluently is useful. Knowing when to question its output is essential.

Kenya’s education system has navigated significant technology transitions before — computer studies, mobile learning, digital content, online classrooms. Each demanded adaptation. Each rewarded the institutions that treated the technology as a tool in service of learning rather than a substitute for it.

AI presents the same challenge at greater speed and scale. The institutions that respond best will be those that teach students not only how to access the technology, but how to question it, use it responsibly and combine it with the one thing no model can replicate: human judgement applied to real consequences.
AI can help Kenyan learners move faster. Education must still teach them how to think.

Northern corridor states to strengthen disease detection at border points
items.description: Regional countries making up the northern transport corridor are seeking to establish an interconnected digital infrastructure that will help in early detection of diseases at the border crossing points along the route.
content: Regional countries making up the northern transport corridor are seeking to establish an interconnected digital infrastructure that will help in early detection of diseases at the border crossing points along the route.
This is expected to help six countries making up the trade route enhance their preparedness for potential disease outbreaks through early detection.
Northern Corridor Transit and Transport Coordination Authority Executive Secretary Dr John Deng says stronger policies and reliable health data along the route are key help improve intra-trade.

According to speakers at the 3 rd Annual Regional Conference on Transport Corridors and Health, the recently observed cases of Ebola in Kenya is a clear sign for regional countries to establish appropriate mechanisms to ensure early detection and response of such diseases at key border crossing points along the northern corridor.
Through the 13 roadside clinics established by NCTTCA in collaboration with North Star Alliance, 27,500 truck drivers have already been screened for Ebola in Kenya since the outbreak was announced.

To support regional trade, NCTTCA says it is also targeting to set up five wellness centres at Kenya, Uganda, Rwanda, DRC, Burundi and South Sudan border points to ensure truck drivers and traders at border points using a single system to help improve response to the diseases.
The conference targets to identify practical solutions to the health challenges facing the region’s transport corridor in a bid to improve health of drivers and facilitate trade.
